title: Next.js
description: Next.js 16 with the App Router: routing, Server and Client Components, data fetching, Cache Components and revalidation, Server Actions, proxy.ts, auth, SEO and deployment. Focused on how things work and what interviewers probe.

chapters.title: App Router Fundamentals
chapters.summary: File-system routing with the app directory: pages, layouts, dynamic segments, route groups and navigation.

lesson.heading: Folders are routes, special files are UI
lesson.body:
In the App Router, each folder inside `app/` is a URL segment. A route becomes publicly reachable only when its folder contains a `page.tsx` (for UI) or a `route.ts` (for an API endpoint). Every other file can be colocated safely: `app/dashboard/chart.tsx` is not a route.

Special files define UI for a segment:
- `layout.tsx`: shared UI that wraps the segment and its children.
- `page.tsx`: the unique UI for the route.
- `loading.tsx`: a Suspense fallback for the segment.
- `error.tsx`: an error boundary for the segment.
- `not-found.tsx`: UI for `notFound()` calls and unmatched URLs.
- `template.tsx`: like a layout but remounts on every navigation.
- `default.tsx`: fallback for parallel route slots.
- `route.ts`: a Route Handler (HTTP endpoint).

Folders starting with an underscore (`_components`) are private and never routed. All components in `app/` are Server Components by default.

code.source:
app/
  layout.tsx          -> root layout (required, renders <html> and <body>)
  page.tsx            -> /
  about/page.tsx      -> /about
  blog/
    layout.tsx        -> wraps every /blog/* page
    page.tsx          -> /blog
    [slug]/page.tsx   -> /blog/hello-world
  _components/        -> private, not a route
  (marketing)/
    pricing/page.tsx  -> /pricing (group name is not in the URL)

lesson.heading: Layouts
lesson.body:
A layout receives `children` and wraps every page below it. Layouts nest: the root layout wraps the blog layout, which wraps the blog page.

The **root layout** is required and must render `<html>` and `<body>`. It is the place for global providers, fonts and metadata defaults.

On navigation between sibling pages, shared layouts **do not re-render or remount**. Their state (an open sidebar, a scroll position in a nav, a video playing) is preserved, and only the changed segment is fetched and rendered. This is called partial rendering. If you need a fresh instance on each navigation, for example to re-run an enter animation or reset a form, use `template.tsx` instead.

Layouts do not receive `searchParams`, because they are shared across navigations that may change the query string without re-rendering the layout.

lesson.heading: Dynamic segments and params
lesson.body:
Wrap a folder name in brackets to capture a segment:
- `[slug]` matches one segment: `/blog/a`.
- `[...slug]` is a catch-all: `/docs/a/b/c` gives `slug: ['a','b','c']`, but does not match `/docs`.
- `[[...slug]]` is an optional catch-all: it also matches `/docs` with `slug` undefined.

Since Next.js 15, `params` and `searchParams` are **Promises**, and Next.js 16 removed the temporary synchronous access. Await them in Server Components, or unwrap with React's `use()` in Client Components. Next.js generates global `PageProps<'/route'>` and `LayoutProps<'/route'>` type helpers for typed params.

lesson.heading: Route groups
lesson.body:
A folder in parentheses, like `(marketing)` or `(shop)`, groups routes without adding a URL segment. Uses:
- Give a set of routes its own layout: `(marketing)/layout.tsx` with a big header, `(app)/layout.tsx` with a sidebar, both at the same URL depth.
- Create **multiple root layouts**: remove the top-level `app/layout.tsx` and add one inside each group. Navigating between different root layouts causes a full page load.
- Organize code by team or feature.

Two groups must not resolve to the same URL, such as `(a)/about/page.tsx` and `(b)/about/page.tsx`; that is a build error.

lesson.heading: Navigation
lesson.body:
`<Link href="/blog">` from `next/link` performs client-side navigation: the browser does not reload, shared layouts stay mounted, and Next.js fetches only the RSC payload for segments that changed. In production, links are **prefetched** when they enter the viewport. For static routes the whole route is prefetched; for dynamic routes, Next.js prefetches down to the nearest `loading.tsx` so the loading state can appear instantly. Next.js 16 adds layout deduplication and incremental prefetching so shared layouts are downloaded once.

Other tools:
- `useRouter()` from `next/navigation` (not `next/router`, which is the Pages Router) for `push`, `replace`, `refresh`, `back`, `prefetch`.
- `usePathname()` and `useSearchParams()` in Client Components.
- `redirect()` and `permanentRedirect()` in Server Components, Server Actions and Route Handlers.
- Native `history.pushState` and `replaceState` integrate with the router, which is useful for updating query strings without a server round trip.

keyPoints: Only folders with page.tsx or route.ts are publicly routable; other files can be colocated.
The root layout is required and renders <html> and <body>.
Layouts persist across navigations and keep state; templates remount.
[slug], [...slug] and [[...slug]] capture one, many, or optionally many segments.
params and searchParams are Promises; await them (sync access was removed in Next.js 16).
Route groups (name) organize routes and layouts without changing URLs.
Link prefetches in production and navigates client-side, fetching only changed segments.

questions.prompt: Which URL renders `app/(shop)/products/[id]/page.tsx`?
questions.explanation: Route group names in parentheses are omitted from the URL; [id] matches any single segment.

questions.prompt: Which folder name matches both /docs and /docs/a/b?
questions.explanation: The optional catch-all [[...slug]] also matches the parent path with no segments. [...slug] requires at least one.

questions.prompt: This code worked in Next.js 14. What is required in Next.js 16?
options: Make the component async and await params (or use(params) in a Client Component)
questions.explanation: params is a Promise since Next.js 15 and the synchronous compatibility access was removed in 16.

questions.prompt: A user navigates from /dashboard/settings to /dashboard/billing. What happens to app/dashboard/layout.tsx?
options: It stays mounted and keeps its state; only the page segment changes
The browser does a full reload
questions.explanation: Partial rendering keeps shared layouts mounted. Use template.tsx if you need a fresh instance per navigation.

questions.prompt: Which import is correct for useRouter in an App Router Client Component?
questions.explanation: next/navigation contains the App Router hooks. next/router is for the Pages Router and does not work in app/.

questions.prompt: Which file is NOT a route on its own?
questions.explanation: Only page and route files expose a segment publicly. Other files in app/ can be safely colocated.

questions.prompt: The root layout must render the <html> and <body> tags.
questions.explanation: Next.js does not inject them. The root layout (or each root layout when using route groups) must include both.

questions.prompt: Layouts receive searchParams as a prop.
questions.explanation: Layouts are shared and not re-rendered on navigation, so they cannot depend on the query string. Use searchParams in the page or useSearchParams in a Client Component.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which are App Router special file conventions?
questions.explanation: _app.tsx and getStaticProps belong to the Pages Router. loading, error, not-found and template are App Router conventions.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: a folder named ___ (with a leading character) is private and excluded from routing, for example _components.
questions.explanation: Prefixing a folder with an underscore opts it and its children out of routing.

questions.prompt: What are the main differences between the App Router and the Pages Router?
questions.answer: The App Router (app/) is built on React Server Components: components are server-rendered by default, can be async and fetch data directly, and ship no JS unless marked 'use client'. Pages Router (pages/) treats every page as a client component, with data loaded via getServerSideProps, getStaticProps and getInitialProps. The App Router adds nested layouts that persist across navigation, file conventions for loading and error states based on Suspense and error boundaries, streaming, Server Actions for mutations, Route Handlers instead of API routes, the Metadata API, and fine-grained caching (use cache, cacheLife, cacheTag in Next 16). Navigation fetches RSC payloads for changed segments only. Pages Router is still supported, and both can coexist during migration.

questions.prompt: Layout vs template: when would you use each?
questions.answer: Both wrap child segments. A layout is mounted once and persists across navigations between its children, preserving state and avoiding re-rendering; it is the default choice for shared chrome like navbars and sidebars. A template creates a new instance for each navigation, so state resets, effects re-run and DOM is recreated. Use a template when you need per-navigation behavior: enter/exit animations, logging a page view in an effect, resetting a form or a feedback widget per page, or Suspense boundaries that should show their fallback on every navigation.

questions.prompt: What happens when a user clicks a Next.js Link?
questions.answer: Link intercepts the click and performs a soft navigation. If the route was prefetched (production links prefetch when they enter the viewport), the RSC payload is already in the client router cache; otherwise Next.js requests it. The server renders only the segments that changed below the shared layout and streams the RSC payload. The router merges it into the existing tree, so shared layouts keep their state, then updates the URL with the History API and manages scroll. If a loading.tsx exists, its fallback shows immediately while dynamic content streams. A navigation that crosses root layouts triggers a full page load instead.

chapters.title: Server and Client Components in Next.js
chapters.summary: Deciding what runs where, placing 'use client' boundaries, passing data across them, and avoiding hydration errors.

lesson.heading: Server by default
lesson.body:
Every component in `app/` is a Server Component unless its module (or a module that imports it) is marked with `'use client'`. Server Components:
- run on the server at build time or request time,
- can be `async` and fetch data, query a database, or read files directly,
- can use secrets, since their code never reaches the browser,
- add zero JavaScript to the client bundle.

They cannot use state, effects, event handlers, browser APIs, or hooks that depend on them. Use a Client Component for those.

lesson.heading: When to use a Client Component
lesson.body:
Add `'use client'` when a component needs:
- state or reducers (`useState`, `useReducer`),
- effects and lifecycle (`useEffect`),
- event handlers (`onClick`, `onChange`),
- browser-only APIs (localStorage, window, geolocation, IntersectionObserver),
- client hooks such as `useRouter`, `usePathname`, `useSearchParams`, or context consumers.

Client Components are still pre-rendered to HTML on the server for the first load, then hydrated in the browser. So 'client' means 'also runs on the client', not 'only runs on the client'.

`'use client'` is a **module boundary**: the file and everything it imports join the client bundle. Put it as low in the tree as possible, on the interactive leaf, not on a whole page.

lesson.heading: Composition across the boundary
lesson.body:
A Client Component cannot import a Server Component (the import would turn it into client code). It can, however, **receive** Server Components as `children` or other JSX props. The server renders them first and passes the result through.

This is how providers work: create a `'use client'` `Providers` component that wraps `children` with ThemeProvider or QueryClientProvider, and render it in the root layout. The pages inside stay Server Components.

Props passed from Server to Client Components must be serializable by React: strings, numbers, booleans, plain objects, arrays, Date, Map, Set, promises, JSX, and Server Functions. Not class instances or ordinary functions.

lesson.heading: Keeping server code on the server
lesson.body:
Environment variables without the `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix are only available on the server; in client bundles they are replaced with empty strings. `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variables are **inlined at build time** into the client bundle, so never put secrets there.

To make sure a module (a database client, a secret-using helper) is never imported into client code, add `import 'server-only'` at the top. Importing it from a Client Component becomes a build error. The `client-only` package does the reverse.

Third-party components that use hooks but lack a `'use client'` directive (older libraries) fail when rendered from a Server Component. Wrap them in your own file with `'use client'` and re-export.

lesson.heading: Hydration errors
lesson.body:
Hydration attaches React to server-rendered HTML. React expects the first client render to produce the same markup as the server. Mismatches cause a hydration error and React re-renders that part on the client. Common causes: - rendering `Date.now()`, `new Date().toLocaleString()` or `Math.random()` directly, - branching on `typeof window !== 'undefined'` during render, - reading localStorage during render, - invalid HTML nesting such as `
` inside `

`, - browser extensions modifying the DOM. Fixes: render the client-only value after mount in a `useEffect`, use `useSyncExternalStore` with a server snapshot, load the component with `dynamic(() => import(...), { ssr: false })` from a Client Component, or for a single unavoidable text difference like a timestamp, add `suppressHydrationWarning` to that element.

keyPoints: Components in app/ are Server Components by default and ship no JavaScript.
Use 'use client' for state, effects, event handlers, browser APIs and client hooks.
'use client' marks a module boundary; place it on interactive leaves.
Client Components can render Server Components passed as children, but cannot import them.
Props crossing the boundary must be serializable.
NEXT_PUBLIC_ env vars are inlined into the client at build time; import 'server-only' guards server modules.
Hydration errors come from server/client output differences such as dates, randomness or window checks.

questions.prompt: What happens when you build this?
options: Error: useState only works in Client Components; add 'use client'
It renders but the click does nothing
questions.explanation: Pages are Server Components by default, where state and event handlers are not available.

questions.prompt: A Client Component needs to display a server-rendered list inside its collapsible panel. What is the correct approach?
options: Import the Server Component inside the Client Component
Pass the Server Component as children from a Server Component parent
Convert the list to a Client Component and fetch in useEffect
questions.explanation: Client Components can render Server Components they receive as props or children. Importing them would make them client code.

questions.prompt: Where does `process.env.STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` resolve in a Client Component?
options: To undefined or empty, since only NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables are exposed to the browser
questions.explanation: Non-public env vars are not inlined into client bundles. Only NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables are, which is why secrets must never use that prefix.

questions.prompt: Why does this cause a hydration error?
options: The server and client compute different times, so the HTML differs
questions.explanation: The server render and the first client render produce different text. Render it after mount or use suppressHydrationWarning for that element.

questions.prompt: What does `import 'server-only'` at the top of lib/db.ts do?
options: Runs the module only at build time
Makes importing the module from Client Component code a build error
Marks its functions as Server Actions
questions.explanation: server-only is a guard package; it fails the build if the module ends up in a client bundle.

questions.prompt: Which prop cannot be passed from a Server Component page to a 'use client' component?
questions.explanation: Ordinary functions are not serializable. Plain objects, Dates and promises are.

questions.prompt: Client Components are rendered only in the browser and never on the server.
questions.explanation: Client Components are pre-rendered to HTML on the server for the initial load and then hydrated.

questions.prompt: Every module imported by a 'use client' file becomes part of the client bundle.
questions.explanation: The directive marks an entry point into client code; its import graph is bundled for the browser.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which require a Client Component?
options: Rendering markdown to HTML on the server
questions.explanation: Event handlers, client hooks and browser APIs need the client. Database access and markdown rendering are ideal server work.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: environment variables are exposed to the browser only if they start with the prefix ___.
questions.explanation: NEXT_PUBLIC_ values are inlined into the client bundle at build time.

questions.prompt: How do you decide whether a component should be a Server or a Client Component?
questions.answer: Default to Server Components: fetching data, accessing backend resources and secrets, rendering static or content-heavy UI, and using large dependencies like markdown or syntax highlighters, which then cost no client JS. Switch to a Client Component only for interactivity and browser features: state, effects, event handlers, browser APIs, and client hooks like useRouter or context. Then minimize the client surface by pushing 'use client' to leaves, and use the children pattern so interactive wrappers like modals or tabs can contain server-rendered content. Providers go in a small client wrapper in the root layout. I pass serializable, minimal props across the boundary rather than whole database rows.

questions.prompt: What is a hydration mismatch and how do you fix one?
questions.answer: Hydration is React attaching event handlers and state to server-rendered HTML; it requires the first client render to match the server output. A mismatch happens when output depends on something that differs between environments: current time, random values, locale formatting, window or localStorage checks during render, invalid HTML nesting the browser repairs, or extensions altering the DOM. React reports it and re-renders that subtree on the client, which costs performance and can flash content. Fix by making the first render deterministic and moving client-only values into an effect or useSyncExternalStore with a server snapshot, disabling SSR for a truly client-only widget with next/dynamic ssr: false, or using suppressHydrationWarning on one element for unavoidable differences like timestamps.

questions.prompt: How do you use a context provider (theme, React Query) in the App Router?
questions.answer: Context requires a Client Component, and the root layout should stay a Server Component. So I create app/providers.tsx with 'use client' that renders ThemeProvider, QueryClientProvider and so on around children, and render <Providers>{children}</Providers> in the root layout. Because children are passed through, the pages inside remain Server Components. For QueryClient I create it with useState(() => new QueryClient()) so each browser session gets one instance and the server does not share one across requests. I render providers as deep as practical, so static parts outside them can be optimized.

chapters.title: Advanced Routing, Loading and Error UI
chapters.summary: Parallel and intercepting routes, loading.tsx and streaming, error.tsx, not-found and redirects.

lesson.heading: loading.tsx and streaming
lesson.body:
`loading.tsx` in a segment automatically wraps that segment's `page` (and nested children) in a `<Suspense>` boundary with the loading component as fallback. The layout above it renders immediately and stays interactive, and the page streams in when its data is ready.

Streaming means the server sends HTML in chunks over one response: the shell first, then each Suspense boundary's content as it resolves, with a small inline script that swaps it into place. Users see something meaningful sooner (better TTFB and FCP), and the slowest query no longer blocks the whole page.

For finer control, place your own `<Suspense>` boundaries around slow components inside a page. Each one can stream independently.

lesson.heading: error.tsx, global-error.tsx and not-found.tsx
lesson.body:
`error.tsx` wraps a segment in an error boundary. It must be a **Client Component** (`'use client'`) because error boundaries are client-side. It receives `error` (with an optional `digest` that matches the server log; production hides server error messages from the client) and `reset()`, which re-renders the segment to try again.

An `error.tsx` catches errors in its segment's page and children, but **not in the layout of the same segment**, because the boundary sits inside that layout. To catch layout errors, place `error.tsx` in the parent segment. Errors in the root layout are handled by `app/global-error.tsx`, which replaces the root layout and therefore must render its own `<html>` and `<body>`.

`notFound()` from `next/navigation` throws a special error that renders the nearest `not-found.tsx`. Unmatched URLs render `app/not-found.tsx`. `redirect()` and `permanentRedirect()` also work by throwing, so do not call them inside a try/catch that swallows the error.

lesson.heading: The component hierarchy of a segment
lesson.body:
For one segment, Next.js nests the special files in a fixed order:

`layout` > `template` > `error` boundary > `loading` Suspense boundary > `not-found` boundary > `page`.

This explains the rules: the layout is outside the error and loading boundaries of its own segment, so a layout error bubbles to the parent's `error.tsx`, and a slow layout is not covered by its own `loading.tsx`.

lesson.heading: Parallel routes
lesson.body:
Parallel routes render several pages in the same layout at once, using **slots**: folders named `@name`. Each slot is passed to the layout as a prop next to `children`. Slots are not URL segments.

Uses: dashboards with independent sections that each have their own loading and error states, conditional rendering (show `@admin` or `@user` based on role), and modals.

When navigating, each slot keeps its active state if the URL does not match it on a soft navigation. On a hard navigation (full load or refresh), Next.js cannot recover the active state and renders the slot's `default.tsx`. In Next.js 16 every slot **must** have an explicit `default.tsx`; builds fail without one. Return `null` or call `notFound()` for the previous behavior.

lesson.heading: Intercepting routes and the modal pattern
lesson.body:
Intercepting routes load a route inside the current layout while the URL changes to that route. The classic example is a photo feed: clicking a photo opens it in a modal over the feed with the URL `/photo/123`, but refreshing or sharing that URL opens the full photo page.

Conventions are relative to **route segments**, not the file system:
- `(.)photo` intercepts a segment at the same level,
- `(..)photo` one level up,
- `(..)(..)photo` two levels up,
- `(...)photo` from the app root.

The common setup combines a parallel `@modal` slot with an intercepting route inside it, plus `@modal/default.tsx` returning `null`. Closing the modal calls `router.back()`. The modal gets shareable URLs, back button behavior and refresh behavior for free.

code.source:
app/
  layout.tsx            -> renders {children} and {modal}
  feed/page.tsx
  photo/[id]/page.tsx   -> full page on direct visit or refresh
  @modal/
    default.tsx         -> returns null
    (.)photo/[id]/page.tsx -> modal version on client navigation

keyPoints: loading.tsx wraps the page in Suspense; the layout renders immediately and content streams in.
Custom Suspense boundaries let independent parts of a page stream separately.
error.tsx must be a Client Component, receives error and reset, and does not catch its own segment's layout errors.
global-error.tsx handles root layout errors and must render <html> and <body>.
notFound(), redirect() and permanentRedirect() work by throwing; keep them out of try/catch.
Parallel routes use @slot folders passed as layout props; Next.js 16 requires default.tsx for every slot.
Intercepting routes ((.), (..), (...)) plus a @modal slot create URL-addressable modals.

questions.prompt: app/dashboard/layout.tsx throws during render. Which file handles it?
questions.explanation: A segment's error boundary sits inside its layout, so layout errors bubble to the parent's error.tsx (or global-error.tsx for the root layout).

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this error file?
options: It must be a Client Component with 'use client'
It must export a named function
questions.explanation: Error boundaries run on the client, so error.tsx requires the 'use client' directive.

questions.prompt: Why does the redirect never happen?
options: redirect only works in Client Components
redirect throws a special error that the catch swallows
questions.explanation: redirect and notFound throw control-flow errors that Next.js handles. Call them outside try/catch or rethrow.

questions.prompt: In Next.js 16, you add an @analytics slot but no default.tsx. What happens?
options: The build fails; every slot needs an explicit default.tsx
questions.explanation: Next.js 16 requires default.js for all parallel route slots. Return null or call notFound() for the old behavior.

questions.prompt: In the photo-modal pattern, the user refreshes the page while the modal URL /photo/7 is open. What renders?
questions.explanation: Interception only applies to soft (client) navigations. A hard load renders the real route.

questions.prompt: Which statement about loading.tsx is correct?
options: It shows only during the first page load
It wraps the segment's page in a Suspense boundary, so the layout stays visible while the page streams
It must be a Client Component
It replaces the layout while loading
questions.explanation: loading.tsx is sugar for a Suspense boundary inside the layout. It is a Server Component by default and is also shown instantly on navigation thanks to prefetching.

questions.prompt: Slots in parallel routes (@name) are part of the URL.
questions.explanation: Slots do not affect the URL. /dashboard/@analytics/page.tsx renders at /dashboard.

questions.prompt: global-error.tsx must render its own <html> and <body> tags.
questions.explanation: It replaces the root layout when active, so it must provide the document structure itself.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: benefits of streaming with Suspense in the App Router.
options: Faster time to first byte and first contentful paint
Slow data no longer blocks the whole page
It removes the need for a database index
Parts of the page can hydrate and become interactive earlier
questions.explanation: Streaming sends the shell early and lets boundaries resolve independently, including selective hydration. It does not speed up queries or cache data.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: to intercept a route at the root of the app directory, prefix the folder with ___.
questions.explanation: (...) matches from the root app directory; (.) is same level and (..) is one segment up.

questions.prompt: How would you build a modal that has its own URL in the App Router?
questions.answer: Use parallel plus intercepting routes. In the layout that should show the modal, add an @modal slot rendered next to children, with @modal/default.tsx returning null so the slot is empty normally. Inside the slot, add an intercepting route like @modal/(.)photo/[id]/page.tsx that renders the photo in a modal component. Also keep the real app/photo/[id]/page.tsx. Clicking a Link to /photo/7 is intercepted and shows the modal over the current page; the URL updates so it is shareable, the back button closes it, and refresh or direct visits render the full page. Closing the modal calls router.back(). Next.js 16 needs default.tsx files for the slot.

questions.prompt: Explain how errors are handled at different levels in the App Router.
questions.answer: Expected errors, such as validation failures or a missing record, should be returned as values or handled with notFound(), not thrown; Server Actions can return error state to useActionState. Unexpected errors are caught by the nearest error.tsx, a client error boundary wrapping a segment's page and children, which gets the error (message hidden in production, digest for log correlation) and a reset function. Because the boundary is inside the layout, layout errors go to the parent's error.tsx, and root layout errors to global-error.tsx, which must render html and body. Event handler and async client errors are not caught by boundaries and need try/catch. I also log server errors centrally with instrumentation.ts and onRequestError.

questions.prompt: Where would you place Suspense boundaries on a product page and why?
questions.answer: I want the shell (header, nav, product title, price, images) to render immediately, ideally from cache. Slower or personalized parts get their own boundaries with skeletons that match their final size to avoid layout shift: reviews, recommendations, stock by store, and the user's cart badge. Related content that should appear together shares a boundary to avoid popcorn loading. I avoid putting one boundary around the whole page because then the slowest query blocks everything, and I avoid wrapping every tiny component because too many skeletons look busy. With Cache Components, anything dynamic must be inside Suspense anyway, so boundaries also define the static shell for Partial Prerendering.

chapters.title: Data Fetching and Rendering Strategies
chapters.summary: Fetching in Server Components, avoiding waterfalls, and how SSG, SSR, ISR and Partial Prerendering map onto the App Router.

lesson.heading: Fetching in Server Components
lesson.body:
In the App Router you fetch where you need the data: an async Server Component can `await` an ORM query, a `fetch` call, or any server function. There is no `getServerSideProps`. Data never has to pass through an API route you control just to reach your own UI.

Deduplication: identical `fetch` calls (same URL and options) in one render pass are memoized by React, so a layout and a page can both request the current user without making two requests. For non-fetch functions such as database calls, wrap them in React's `cache()` to get the same per-request deduplication.

Client-side fetching is still valid for highly interactive, user-specific data that changes after load, typically with TanStack Query or SWR, or by passing a promise from a Server Component and reading it with `use()`.

lesson.heading: Sequential vs parallel fetching
lesson.body:
Awaiting one request after another creates a **waterfall**: total time is the sum of all requests. When requests are independent, start them together and await them with `Promise.all` (or `Promise.allSettled` if one may fail without breaking the page).

Waterfalls also appear across components: a parent awaits data, then renders a child that awaits its own data. Sometimes that is intentional (the child needs the parent's result). Otherwise, start fetches higher up and pass promises down, or split the UI into sibling Suspense boundaries so each part fetches in parallel and streams on its own.

lesson.heading: Static and dynamic rendering
lesson.body:
Next.js renders routes in two basic ways.

- **Static (prerendered)**: HTML and the RSC payload are produced at build time or during revalidation, then served from cache or a CDN. This is SSG. Fastest and cheapest.
- **Dynamic**: rendered per request on the server. This is SSR. Required when output depends on the request.

A route becomes dynamic when it uses request-time data: `cookies()`, `headers()`, `searchParams`, `connection()`, `draftMode()`, or uncached data. In Next.js 15 and later, `fetch` is not cached by default.

`generateStaticParams` returns the list of params to prerender for a dynamic route at build time, so `/blog/[slug]` can be fully static for known posts. With `export const dynamicParams = false`, any other slug returns 404; with the default `true`, unknown slugs render on demand and are then cached.

lesson.heading: ISR: static with revalidation
lesson.body:
Incremental Static Regeneration keeps pages static but refreshes them after deployment. Two kinds of revalidation:
- **Time-based**: after a lifetime expires, the next request still gets the cached (stale) page while Next.js regenerates it in the background. In Next 16 with Cache Components this is `cacheLife('hours')` inside `'use cache'`; in the earlier model it is `export const revalidate = 3600` or `fetch(url, { next: { revalidate: 3600 } })`.
- **On-demand**: after a mutation or a CMS webhook, call `revalidateTag`, `updateTag` or `revalidatePath` to invalidate specific data or pages.

ISR gives most of SSG's speed with fresh enough content, which suits product catalogs, blogs and docs.

lesson.heading: Partial Prerendering and Cache Components
lesson.body:
Most pages are mostly static with a few dynamic parts: a product page with a personalized cart badge, for example. Without PPR, one dynamic bit made the whole route dynamic.

**Partial Prerendering (PPR)** prerenders a static shell of the route and leaves holes for dynamic parts, defined by `<Suspense>` boundaries. The shell is served instantly from the edge; the dynamic parts stream into the same response.

In Next.js 16, PPR is delivered through **Cache Components** (`cacheComponents: true` in `next.config.ts`; the old `experimental.ppr` flag was removed). The model is: everything is dynamic by default; mark cacheable parts with `'use cache'`; anything that reads request data or uncached data must sit inside a `<Suspense>` boundary, otherwise the build reports an error asking you to either cache it or wrap it. Route segment configs like `export const dynamic` and `revalidate` are replaced by this model when Cache Components is on.

keyPoints: Fetch data directly in async Server Components; no getServerSideProps in the App Router.
fetch calls are memoized per render; wrap DB calls in React cache() for the same deduplication.
Avoid waterfalls with Promise.all and sibling Suspense boundaries.
Request-time APIs (cookies, headers, searchParams, connection) make rendering dynamic.
generateStaticParams prerenders dynamic routes; dynamicParams = false 404s unknown params.
ISR serves stale content while regenerating, plus on-demand invalidation after mutations.
Next.js 16 delivers PPR through cacheComponents: a cached static shell with dynamic Suspense holes.

questions.prompt: Each call takes about 500 ms. How long does this page take to get its data?
questions.explanation: Each await waits for the previous one: a waterfall. Promise.all would bring it to about 500 ms because the calls are independent.

questions.prompt: In Next.js 15 and 16, is `await fetch('https://api.example.com/posts')` cached across requests by default?
options: No, fetch is not cached by default
Only for GET requests in Route Handlers
questions.explanation: Next.js 15 changed the default to no caching. Opt in with 'use cache' (Cache Components) or cache: 'force-cache' / next.revalidate in the earlier model.

questions.prompt: A layout and a page both call getCurrentUser(), which queries Prisma. How do you avoid two DB queries per request?
options: Put the user in a global variable
Call it only in the layout and pass it via context
questions.explanation: React cache() memoizes a function per server request. Global variables would leak data between users.

questions.prompt: With `dynamicParams = false` and generateStaticParams returning slugs a and b, what does /blog/c return?
questions.explanation: dynamicParams = false restricts the route to the generated params; others return a 404.

questions.prompt: With cacheComponents enabled, a component reads cookies() and is not inside any Suspense boundary. What happens?
options: The whole route silently becomes dynamic
Next.js reports an error asking you to wrap it in Suspense or move the data access
The component is cached per user automatically
questions.explanation: Cache Components requires request-time data to sit behind a Suspense boundary so the rest can be prerendered as a static shell.

questions.prompt: With time-based ISR, a request arrives after the page's revalidation time has passed. What does that user get?
options: They wait for the fresh page
The stale cached page, while regeneration happens in the background
questions.explanation: ISR uses stale-while-revalidate: the expired page is served once more and the next visitor sees the regenerated version.

questions.prompt: Using searchParams in a page makes that page dynamically rendered.
questions.explanation: searchParams are only known at request time, so the page cannot be fully prerendered (with PPR the static shell can still be served).

questions.prompt: In the App Router you should call your own Route Handler with fetch from a Server Component to get data.
questions.explanation: That adds an extra HTTP hop (and fails at build time since no server is running). Call the data function directly from the Server Component.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which APIs opt rendering into request time?
questions.explanation: generateStaticParams runs at build time to prerender pages. The others read request data or explicitly wait for a request.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the next.config option that enables Cache Components and PPR in Next.js 16 is ___: true.
questions.explanation: cacheComponents replaced experimental.ppr and experimental.dynamicIO.

questions.prompt: Explain SSG, SSR, ISR and PPR and when you would choose each.
questions.answer: SSG renders at build time and serves static files from a CDN: fastest, cheapest, good for marketing pages and docs that change with deploys. SSR renders on every request: needed when output depends on the request (cookies, auth, search params) or must be real-time, at the cost of server time and TTFB. ISR is static plus revalidation: pages are regenerated after a lifetime with stale-while-revalidate, or on demand via tags or paths after a CMS webhook or mutation; good for catalogs, blogs and listings. PPR mixes them inside one route: a prerendered static shell served instantly with Suspense holes streamed per request, ideal for mostly-static pages with personalized bits like a cart or recommendations. In Next.js 16, PPR comes from Cache Components: dynamic by default, opt into caching with 'use cache' and cacheLife.

questions.prompt: How do you avoid data fetching waterfalls in the App Router?
questions.answer: First, start independent requests together with Promise.all instead of sequential awaits. Second, avoid component waterfalls where a parent awaits before rendering a child that then fetches: split independent parts into sibling components each wrapped in its own Suspense boundary so they fetch and stream in parallel. Third, start a fetch early and pass the promise down (to a Server Component that awaits it or a Client Component that calls use()). Fourth, use preload patterns: call a cached data function early (void getItem(id)) so it is in flight when a child needs it. Also check the network side: colocate the server near the database and batch queries where possible.

questions.prompt: When would you still fetch data on the client in an App Router app?
questions.answer: When data is highly interactive or changes after the initial render: infinite scroll, live search suggestions, polling dashboards, real-time feeds, optimistic UIs with frequent mutations, or user-specific widgets on otherwise static pages that I do not want to make dynamic. I would use TanStack Query or SWR for caching, deduping, background refetching and retries, often seeding it with initial data from a Server Component (prefetch plus HydrationBoundary). Data that is needed for the first paint, SEO, or uses secrets I fetch on the server. Client fetching that calls your own Route Handlers also needs auth checks there.

chapters.title: Server Actions and Route Handlers
chapters.summary: Mutating data with Server Actions, revalidating after writes, and building HTTP endpoints with Route Handlers.

lesson.heading: Defining Server Actions
lesson.body:
A Server Action is an async function marked with `'use server'` that runs on the server and can be called from the client. Two ways to define them:
- Inline, as the first statement of an async function inside a Server Component.
- File-level, with `'use server'` at the top of a module such as `app/actions.ts`. Every export becomes a Server Action, and Client Components can import them.

Client Components cannot define inline Server Actions, but they can import them or receive them as props.

Under the hood, Next.js gives each action an ID. Calling it sends a POST request to the current route with the ID and serialized arguments; the response contains the return value and, if you revalidated, the updated RSC payload for the page, all in one round trip.

lesson.heading: Calling Server Actions
lesson.body:
- `<form action={createPost}>`: the action receives `FormData`. In a Server Component this works before JavaScript loads (progressive enhancement).
- With `useActionState(createPost, initialState)` in a Client Component to get returned state (validation errors) and `isPending`.
- `<button formAction={otherAction}>` for multiple submit buttons.
- From an event handler or effect: `startTransition(async () => { await likePost(id); })`.
- Extra arguments: `createPost.bind(null, postId)` to pre-fill arguments while keeping progressive enhancement.

Actions are designed for **mutations**. The client dispatches them one at a time, so they are a poor fit for parallel data fetching; read data in Server Components or with a client cache instead.

lesson.heading: Revalidating and redirecting after a mutation
lesson.body:
After writing data you must tell Next.js which cached UI is stale:
- `revalidatePath('/posts')` invalidates a route (optionally `'layout'` type for a whole subtree).
- `updateTag('posts')` (Next 16, Server Actions only) expires tagged cache entries so the response already includes fresh data: read-your-own-writes.
- `revalidateTag('posts', 'max')` marks tagged entries stale with stale-while-revalidate semantics; good for webhooks where eventual consistency is fine.
- `refresh()` (Next 16, Server Actions only) re-renders uncached dynamic data without touching caches.
- `redirect('/somewhere')` navigates after the action; it throws, so call it after the try/catch.

When revalidation happens inside an action, Next.js returns the new UI in the same response, so the page updates without an extra request.

lesson.heading: Server Action security
lesson.body:
Every exported Server Action is a reachable POST endpoint, even if no UI calls it. Treat it like an API route.

- **Validate** every argument with a schema; TypeScript types are not runtime checks.
- **Authenticate and authorize inside the action**, not just in the page or layout that renders the form. Ideally through a shared data access layer.
- Next.js compares the `Origin` header with the `Host` to block cross-site requests (CSRF); allow extra origins with `serverActions.allowedOrigins` when behind proxies.
- Closed-over variables in inline actions are encrypted when sent to the client, and action IDs change between builds; unused actions are removed from the bundle. Still, do not close over secrets.
- Request bodies are limited (1 MB by default, `serverActions.bodySizeLimit`).
- Add rate limiting for expensive or abuse-prone actions.

lesson.heading: Route Handlers
lesson.body:
A `route.ts` file exports functions named after HTTP methods (`GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`) using the Web `Request` and `Response` APIs, extended by `NextRequest` and `NextResponse`. A `route.ts` cannot live in the same segment as a `page.tsx`.

Use Route Handlers for things that are not your own React UI: webhooks (Stripe, a CMS), endpoints consumed by mobile apps or third parties, OAuth callbacks, file downloads, RSS or sitemap feeds, and streaming responses. For mutations triggered by your own UI, Server Actions are usually simpler.

Since Next.js 15, `GET` handlers are not cached by default. Like pages, dynamic params arrive as a Promise in the second argument.

keyPoints: 'use server' marks Server Actions inline in Server Components or for every export of a file.
Actions are POST requests by ID; they return values and updated UI in one round trip.
Forms with action={serverAction} work before hydration (progressive enhancement).
After writes, call revalidatePath, updateTag, revalidateTag(tag, profile) or refresh().
Every action is a public endpoint: validate input and check auth inside it.
Server Actions are for mutations; they are dispatched sequentially, so do not use them for fetching.
Route Handlers (route.ts) serve webhooks, external clients and non-UI endpoints; GET is uncached by default.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this Client Component?
options: Client Components cannot define inline Server Actions; import them from a 'use server' file
questions.explanation: Inline 'use server' functions are only allowed in Server Components. Put the action in a separate file and import it.

questions.prompt: Which HTTP method does Next.js use to invoke a Server Action?
questions.explanation: Actions are invoked with POST requests carrying the action ID and serialized arguments.

questions.prompt: After a user saves their profile in a Server Action, they must see the new values immediately. Which Next 16 API fits best?
questions.explanation: updateTag expires the entries immediately for read-your-own-writes. revalidateTag with a profile uses stale-while-revalidate, so the user could briefly see old data.

questions.prompt: You add app/dashboard/route.ts next to app/dashboard/page.tsx. What happens?
options: GET goes to route.ts, others to page
Conflict error: a segment cannot have both
questions.explanation: A segment can be a page or a Route Handler, not both. Put APIs under a different path such as app/api/dashboard/route.ts.

questions.prompt: The delete form is only rendered for admins. Is this action secure?
options: Yes, only admins see the button
No, anyone can call the action endpoint; it must verify the session and role itself
questions.explanation: Hiding UI is not authorization. The action is a POST endpoint reachable by any client, so it must authenticate and authorize.

questions.prompt: Which is the best use of a Route Handler rather than a Server Action?
options: Toggling a todo from a button
questions.explanation: Webhooks come from third parties calling a stable URL with their own payload format. The other cases are UI mutations that suit Server Actions.

questions.prompt: A form whose action is a Server Action can submit even before the page's JavaScript has loaded, when rendered from a Server Component.
questions.explanation: The form is a real HTML form posting to the server, which is progressive enhancement.

questions.prompt: Server Actions are a good way to fetch data in parallel for a Client Component.
questions.explanation: Actions are dispatched one at a time by the client and designed for mutations. Fetch in Server Components or with a client data library.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: what should every Server Action that writes data do?
options: Validate inputs with a runtime schema
Return the full database row including internal fields
questions.explanation: Types vanish at runtime and full rows can leak data. Validation, auth checks and cache invalidation are required.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: to invalidate all cached data for the route /posts after a mutation, call ___('/posts').
questions.explanation: revalidatePath invalidates the cached output of a path; use tag APIs for finer-grained data invalidation.

questions.prompt: Server Actions vs Route Handlers: how do you choose?
questions.answer: Server Actions are for mutations initiated by my own React UI. They give type-safe function calls without designing endpoints, progressive enhancement for forms, integration with useActionState and useOptimistic, and they can revalidate and return the updated RSC payload in a single round trip. Route Handlers are for HTTP endpoints with a stable public contract: webhooks, mobile or third-party clients, OAuth callbacks, file downloads, feeds, and streaming responses. Actions are not good for data fetching because they are POST, uncached and dispatched sequentially. Both are public endpoints, so both need validation, authentication, authorization and rate limiting.

questions.prompt: Walk through what happens when a user submits a form bound to a Server Action that calls revalidatePath and redirect.
questions.answer: The browser, or React if hydrated, sends a POST to the current URL with the action ID header and the FormData. If hydrated, React runs it inside a transition, so useFormStatus and useActionState report pending. On the server, Next.js finds the action by ID, checks the Origin against the Host, decodes arguments and runs the function: it validates, checks auth, writes to the database, then revalidatePath marks the route's cached output stale. redirect throws a redirect signal, so Next.js responds with the RSC payload for the target route, rendered fresh because of the revalidation. The client router applies it and updates the URL, all in one round trip. Without JavaScript, the form posts normally and the server responds with a redirect.

questions.prompt: How do you return validation errors from a Server Action to the form?
questions.answer: I define the action with the useActionState signature (prevState, formData), validate with a schema like Zod using safeParse, and on failure return a serializable object such as { errors: fieldErrors, values } instead of throwing. Thrown errors are for unexpected failures and would hit the error boundary. In the Client Component, useActionState(action, initialState) gives me state for rendering per-field messages, a formAction for the form, and isPending for the button. I return submitted values so inputs can be repopulated via defaultValue, because React resets uncontrolled forms after a successful action. Client-side validation (HTML constraints or React Hook Form) is a UX layer on top, never a replacement for server validation.

chapters.title: Metadata, SEO, Images and Fonts
chapters.summary: The Metadata API, OG images, sitemaps and robots, and the built-in image, font and script optimizations.

lesson.heading: Static and dynamic metadata
lesson.body:
Export a `metadata` object from a layout or page for static metadata, or an async `generateMetadata` function when it depends on params or data. Both are only supported in Server Components.

Metadata from nested segments is merged from the root down. Nested objects like `openGraph` are **replaced**, not deep-merged, by the deeper segment, so define shared Open Graph fields in a variable and spread them.

`title.template` in a layout (for example `'%s | Acme'`) formats child titles, and `title.default` is used when a child sets none. Set `metadataBase` in the root layout so relative URLs in Open Graph images and canonicals resolve to absolute URLs.

Data fetched in `generateMetadata` and in the page is deduplicated when you use `fetch` or React `cache()`, so you do not pay twice for the same post.

lesson.heading: File-based metadata
lesson.body:
Special files generate metadata automatically:
- `favicon.ico`, `icon.png`, `apple-icon.png` (or `icon.tsx` to generate one).
- `opengraph-image.png|tsx` and `twitter-image.png|tsx` per segment. The `.tsx` versions use `ImageResponse` from `next/og` to render JSX to a PNG at build or request time.
- `sitemap.ts` returning a list of URLs, `robots.ts` returning crawl rules, and `manifest.ts` for a web app manifest.

Structured data (JSON-LD) is added by rendering a `<script type="application/ld+json">` in the page with `JSON.stringify` of the schema object (escape `<` characters to prevent injection).

lesson.heading: next/image
lesson.body: The `Image` component extends `` with: - automatic resizing and modern formats (WebP by default, AVIF opt-in) served from the image optimization endpoint, - responsive `srcset` generation based on `sizes`, - lazy loading by default, - reserved space to prevent layout shift (CLS): provide `width` and `height`, or use `fill` inside a positioned parent. Gotchas: - Remote images must be allowed with `images.remotePatterns` (`images.domains` is deprecated in Next 16). - With `fill` or responsive layouts, set `sizes` (for example `"(max-width: 768px) 100vw, 33vw"`), otherwise the browser assumes 100vw and downloads oversized images. - For the LCP image above the fold, do not lazy load it: use `loading="eager"` or `fetchPriority="high"`, or `preload`. In Next.js 16 the old `priority` prop is deprecated in favor of `preload`. - Next 16 defaults: `qualities` is `[75]`, `minimumCacheTTL` is 4 hours, and local images with query strings need `images.localPatterns`.

lesson.heading: next/font
lesson.body:
`next/font/google` and `next/font/local` download font files at **build time** and self-host them with your static assets. The browser never contacts Google, which helps privacy and avoids an extra connection. Next.js also generates a fallback font with adjusted metrics (`size-adjust`), which eliminates layout shift when the web font swaps in.

Use the `variable` option to expose the font as a CSS variable and wire it into Tailwind or your CSS. Load fonts once in the root layout and only the weights and subsets you need.

lesson.heading: next/script and third parties
lesson.body:
`<Script>` from `next/script` loads third-party scripts with a strategy:
- `beforeInteractive`: before hydration (rare: bot detection, consent managers); must be in the root layout.
- `afterInteractive` (default): after some hydration, for tag managers and analytics.
- `lazyOnload`: during browser idle time, for chat widgets and social embeds.
- `worker` (experimental): offloads to a web worker via Partytown.

Scripts are loaded once even when navigating between pages that include them. The `@next/third-parties` package offers optimized components for Google Tag Manager, Google Analytics, YouTube embeds and Maps.

keyPoints: Use the metadata export or async generateMetadata in Server Components; nested objects like openGraph are replaced, not merged.
title.template formats child titles; metadataBase makes relative URLs absolute.
opengraph-image.tsx, icon.tsx, sitemap.ts, robots.ts and manifest.ts generate metadata from files.
next/image resizes, serves modern formats, lazy loads and prevents CLS; set sizes for responsive images.
Do not lazy load the LCP image; in Next 16 priority is deprecated in favor of preload, loading="eager" or fetchPriority.
next/font self-hosts fonts at build time and adjusts fallbacks to avoid layout shift.
next/script strategies control when third-party scripts load.

questions.prompt: The root layout sets title.template to '%s | Acme'. A page exports `metadata = { title: 'Pricing' }`. What is the document title?
questions.explanation: Child titles are inserted into the nearest parent template.

questions.prompt: The layout defines openGraph with siteName and images. A page defines openGraph: { title: 'Post' }. What does the page's final openGraph contain?
questions.explanation: Metadata merging is shallow: a nested object defined by a deeper segment replaces the parent's object entirely.

questions.prompt: Why might this image download a huge file on mobile?
options: Without sizes, the browser assumes the image is 100vw wide and picks a large srcset candidate
questions.explanation: sizes tells the browser the rendered width; for a one-third-width tile, something like sizes="33vw" picks a much smaller file.

questions.prompt: What does next/font/google do at build time?
options: Downloads and self-hosts the font files, plus generates a metric-adjusted fallback
Inlines fonts as base64 in every page
questions.explanation: Fonts are served from your own domain, so there is no request to Google and no layout shift from the swap.

questions.prompt: Where can generateMetadata be exported?
questions.explanation: The Metadata API is supported only in Server Component layouts and pages.

questions.prompt: A chat widget script is not needed until the user is idle. Which Script strategy fits?
questions.explanation: lazyOnload loads during idle time so it does not compete with critical resources.

questions.prompt: In Next.js 16, the priority prop on next/image is deprecated in favor of preload.
questions.explanation: Next 16 deprecated priority. The docs also recommend loading="eager" or fetchPriority="high" for most LCP images.

questions.prompt: Remote images from any domain work with next/image without configuration.
questions.explanation: Remote hosts must be allowed via images.remotePatterns to prevent abuse of the optimization endpoint.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which files does Next.js treat as metadata conventions?
questions.explanation: sitemap, robots, opengraph-image and icon are conventions. seo.config.ts has no special meaning.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: set ___ in the root layout's metadata so relative Open Graph image URLs become absolute.
questions.explanation: metadataBase is the base URL for URL-based metadata fields.

questions.prompt: How would you set up SEO for a dynamic blog in the App Router?
questions.answer: In the root layout: metadataBase, a title template and default description, and default Open Graph fields. In app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx, generateMetadata fetches the post (deduped with the page through React cache or fetch memoization) and returns title, description, canonical URL via alternates, and Open Graph and Twitter fields. An opengraph-image.tsx in the segment renders a branded OG image with ImageResponse. app/sitemap.ts lists all posts with lastModified, and app/robots.ts points to it and disallows private areas. I add Article JSON-LD in a script tag. Pages are prerendered with generateStaticParams and kept fresh with cacheLife and cacheTag invalidated by the CMS webhook, so crawlers get fast, complete HTML.

questions.prompt: How does next/image improve Core Web Vitals, and what mistakes still hurt them?
questions.answer: It improves LCP by serving resized images in modern formats with responsive srcset, and CLS by reserving space from width and height or a fill container. It improves overall load by lazy loading offscreen images. Common mistakes: lazy loading the hero image (the LCP element), which delays it, so mark it eager or high fetch priority (preload in Next 16, which deprecated priority); missing sizes on fill or responsive images, which downloads desktop-sized files on phones; using huge source images with high quality settings; and not configuring remotePatterns or a CDN loader for remote assets. Next 16 defaults to quality 75 only and a 4-hour minimumCacheTTL.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between static metadata and generateMetadata, and how does streaming affect metadata?
questions.answer: Static metadata is an exported object, resolved at build time, best for fixed pages. generateMetadata is an async function that receives params and searchParams and can fetch data, needed when titles or images depend on content. Data requests are deduplicated with the page render. Since Next.js 15.2, metadata from generateMetadata can be streamed: for regular browsers the page UI does not wait for metadata to resolve, and the tags are injected when ready, while for bots that expect metadata in the head (detected by user agent) Next.js blocks until metadata is ready so crawlers see complete HTML. Both must be in Server Components.
