chapters.title: Caching and Revalidation in Next.js 16
chapters.summary: The caching layers, Cache Components with 'use cache', cacheLife and cacheTag, and choosing between revalidateTag, updateTag, revalidatePath and refresh.

lesson.heading: Why caching changed
lesson.body:
Early App Router versions (13 and 14) cached aggressively and implicitly: `fetch` results, full routes and client router segments were cached by default, which surprised many developers with stale data. Next.js 15 flipped the defaults: `fetch` is uncached, GET Route Handlers are uncached, and the client router cache no longer keeps page segments for dynamic routes (stale time 0).

Next.js 16 introduces **Cache Components**, enabled with `cacheComponents: true`. The model is explicit: all code runs at request time by default, and you opt into caching with the `'use cache'` directive. The older APIs (`fetch` cache options, `export const revalidate`, `unstable_cache`) still exist for apps not using Cache Components, so you will see both in real codebases.

lesson.heading: The caching layers
lesson.body:
- **Request memoization** (React): identical `fetch` calls and `cache()`-wrapped functions are deduplicated within a single server render. It lasts only for that request.
- **'use cache' entries** (server): the output of a cached function or component, stored by a cache handler (in memory by default) and reused across requests until it revalidates or expires. Prerendered entries become part of the route's static shell.
- **Static shell / prerendered output**: HTML and RSC payload produced at build time or on revalidation and served from the CDN.
- **Client router cache** (browser): RSC payloads of visited and prefetched segments kept in memory for back/forward and instant navigation. Its lifetime follows the `stale` time of `cacheLife` (minimum 30 seconds for cached content).

When debugging stale data, ask which layer is serving it.

lesson.heading: 'use cache' in practice
lesson.body:
Put `'use cache'` at the top of a file (every export cached), a component, or an async function. Cached functions must be async.

The **cache key** is generated automatically from the build ID, a hash of the function's location, its serializable arguments (props for components) and any closed-over variables. Different arguments produce different entries, so you do not manage keys by hand.

Constraints:
- No request-time APIs inside: `cookies()`, `headers()` and `searchParams` throw. Read them outside and pass the value (for example a user id) as an argument.
- Arguments and return values must be serializable. `children` and Server Actions can be passed through without being inspected, which lets a cached layout wrap dynamic content (interleaving).
- With the default in-memory handler on serverless platforms, runtime entries may not persist between instances; `'use cache: remote'` uses a platform cache handler, and `'use cache: private'` exists for rare cases that must read request data.

lesson.heading: cacheLife profiles
lesson.body:
`cacheLife(profile)` sets three timings:
- **stale**: how long the client may use the cached value without checking the server.
- **revalidate**: after this, the next request gets the cached value while a fresh one is generated in the background.
- **expire**: after this with no traffic, the entry is dropped and the next request waits for fresh data.

Built-in profiles: `'seconds'`, `'minutes'`, `'hours'`, `'days'`, `'weeks'`, `'max'`, and `'default'` (stale 5 minutes, revalidate 15 minutes, no time-based expiry), which applies if you omit `cacheLife`. Define custom profiles in `next.config.ts` under `cacheLife`, or pass an inline object. Very short lifetimes (like `'seconds'`) are not included in the prerendered shell and resolve at request time instead. Prefer calling `cacheLife` explicitly in every cached scope so the behavior is visible at the call site.

lesson.heading: Invalidation: which API when
lesson.body:
- `cacheTag('posts')` labels a cached entry so it can be invalidated on demand.
- `updateTag('posts')`: Server Actions only. Expires the entries immediately so the same response renders fresh data. Use it when the user must see their own change (read-your-own-writes).
- `revalidateTag('posts', 'max')`: marks entries stale with stale-while-revalidate behavior. Use it in Route Handlers for webhooks or when eventual consistency is fine. In Next 16 the second argument (a cacheLife profile or `{ expire }`) is required; the single-argument form is deprecated.
- `revalidatePath('/blog')`: invalidates by route rather than by data.
- `refresh()`: Server Actions only. Re-renders uncached, dynamic data (like a notification count) without touching any cache.
- `router.refresh()`: client side; re-requests the current route's RSC payload.

keyPoints: Next 15 made fetch and GET Route Handlers uncached by default; Next 16 Cache Components make caching opt-in with 'use cache'.
Layers: request memoization, 'use cache' entries, the prerendered static shell, and the client router cache.
Cache keys come from build ID, function identity, serializable arguments and closed-over values.
cookies(), headers() and searchParams cannot be read inside 'use cache'; pass values in as arguments.
cacheLife sets stale, revalidate and expire; the default profile is 5 min stale, 15 min revalidate.
updateTag gives read-your-own-writes in Server Actions; revalidateTag(tag, profile) gives stale-while-revalidate.
refresh() re-renders uncached data from a Server Action without touching caches.

questions.prompt: What happens with this cached function?
options: It caches per cookie value automatically
It errors: request-time APIs cannot be used inside 'use cache'
It caches the first user's dashboard for everyone
questions.explanation: cookies() and headers() are forbidden in cached scopes. Read the cookie outside and pass the user id as an argument so it becomes part of the key.

questions.prompt: How many cache entries does this produce after calls getPrice('a'), getPrice('b'), getPrice('a')?
questions.explanation: Arguments are part of the key: one entry for 'a' (reused on the third call) and one for 'b'.

questions.prompt: A user edits their bio in a Server Action and must see it on the very next render. Which call is right?
questions.explanation: updateTag expires immediately for read-your-own-writes. revalidateTag with a profile serves stale content once while revalidating.

questions.prompt: In Next.js 16, what is the status of `revalidateTag('posts')` with one argument?
options: Deprecated; pass a cacheLife profile such as 'max' as the second argument, or use updateTag in actions
questions.explanation: Next 16 requires a profile for stale-while-revalidate semantics and deprecates the single-argument form.

questions.prompt: A 'use cache' function has no cacheLife call. Which profile applies?
options: default: stale 5 minutes, revalidate 15 minutes, no time-based expiry
questions.explanation: The default profile applies when cacheLife is omitted. Explicit cacheLife calls are recommended for clarity.

questions.prompt: A header shows an unread notification count read from the database without caching. After markAsRead() in a Server Action, which call updates it without invalidating any caches?
questions.explanation: refresh() re-renders uncached dynamic data and leaves cached content alone.

questions.prompt: Functions and components that use 'use cache' must be async.
questions.explanation: Cached scopes are async so their results can be stored and restored from the cache handler.

questions.prompt: In Next.js 15 and later, GET Route Handlers are cached by default.
questions.explanation: Next.js 15 changed GET handlers to uncached by default, together with fetch.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which become part of a 'use cache' entry's key?
options: Variables captured from an outer scope
A hash of the function's location
questions.explanation: Cookies are not available in cached scopes at all; pass the value you need as an argument.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: to label a cached entry so it can be invalidated later, call ___('products') inside the 'use cache' scope.
questions.explanation: cacheTag associates tags with the entry; updateTag and revalidateTag invalidate by tag.

questions.prompt: Explain the caching model in Next.js 16 compared with Next.js 14.
questions.answer: Next 14 cached implicitly: fetch was force-cache by default, routes were statically rendered unless a dynamic API opted out, and the client router cache held segments for 30 seconds even for dynamic pages, so stale data surprised people. Next 15 made fetch, GET Route Handlers and dynamic page segments in the client cache uncached by default. Next 16 adds Cache Components: with cacheComponents enabled, everything runs at request time unless you mark it with 'use cache' on a file, component or function. Keys are generated by the compiler from arguments and closures, lifetimes come from cacheLife profiles (stale, revalidate, expire), and invalidation uses cacheTag with updateTag (immediate, Server Actions), revalidateTag(tag, profile) (stale-while-revalidate) or revalidatePath. It also powers Partial Prerendering: cached parts form the static shell, dynamic parts stream inside Suspense.

questions.prompt: How would you cache an e-commerce product page that has shared content and per-user content?
questions.answer: With Cache Components on, the product details, images, specs and review summary are fetched in functions or components with 'use cache', cacheLife('hours') or 'days', and tags like product-123 and products. Those parts land in the static shell, prerendered for top products with generateStaticParams. Per-user parts (cart count, personalized price, wishlist state) read cookies, so they live in components inside Suspense boundaries and stream per request. If a personalized part is expensive, I read the user id outside and pass it into a cached function so entries are per user. Admin edits run Server Actions that call updateTag('product-123'); inventory or CMS webhooks call revalidateTag(tag, 'max'). Stock that must be live stays uncached and can be refreshed via refresh().

questions.prompt: Users report seeing stale data after a mutation. How do you debug it?
questions.answer: First identify which layer is stale. If a hard refresh fixes it, it is the client router cache: the mutation did not revalidate, or it ran outside a Server Action so the router was not told; use updateTag or revalidatePath inside the action, or router.refresh() after a client-side mutation. If a hard refresh still shows old data, it is a server cache: check that the cached function has the right cacheTag, that the invalidation uses the same tag string, and whether revalidateTag's stale-while-revalidate behavior explains one stale response. Then check deployment: on multiple self-hosted instances the default in-memory cache is per instance, so you need a shared cache handler. NEXT_PRIVATE_DEBUG_CACHE=1 logs cache activity, and checking response headers shows whether the CDN served it.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between React cache() and 'use cache'?
questions.answer: React cache() memoizes a function for the duration of a single server request. It deduplicates calls, for example getUser in both a layout and a page, and is discarded when the request ends. It works with any data, including per-user data, and needs no serialization. 'use cache' is a Next.js persistent cache: results are stored by a cache handler and reused across requests and users until they revalidate or expire, keys are derived from serialized arguments, and request APIs like cookies are forbidden inside. They are complementary: cache() for per-request dedupe of session and auth lookups, 'use cache' for shared data that is expensive to compute. React cache() storage is also isolated inside 'use cache' scopes, so it cannot be used to pass data into them.

chapters.title: proxy.ts, Authentication and Authorization
chapters.summary: Intercepting requests with proxy.ts (formerly middleware), session strategies, and where auth checks must live.

lesson.heading: proxy.ts replaces middleware.ts
lesson.body:
Next.js 16 renamed `middleware.ts` to `proxy.ts` to make the network boundary explicit, and the exported function is named `proxy` (default export also works). It lives at the project root or in `src/`, one per project, and runs **before** routes and cached content are matched for every request that passes the `matcher`.

`proxy.ts` runs on the **Node.js runtime**. The old `middleware.ts` still works for Edge runtime use cases but is deprecated. A codemod (`npx @next/codemod@canary middleware-to-proxy .`) renames files and config flags.

Good uses:
- redirects and rewrites (legacy URLs, i18n locale detection, A/B test buckets),
- setting request or response headers (security headers, CSP nonces),
- optimistic auth checks: is there a session cookie? If not, redirect to /login.

Bad uses: slow data fetching, database-backed session validation on every request, and being the **only** auth check. Proxy runs on every matched request, including prefetches, so keep it fast.

lesson.heading: Why proxy must not be your only line of defense
lesson.body:
In March 2025, CVE-2025-29927 showed that a crafted `x-middleware-subrequest` header could make Next.js skip middleware entirely on self-hosted deployments. Apps whose only authorization lived in middleware were fully exposed. The lesson generalizes: checks at the edge of the app are **optimistic** filters for UX and performance. Real authorization must happen next to the data, in every Server Component, Server Action and Route Handler that reads or writes protected data.

The same applies to layouts. Because layouts do not re-render on client navigation (partial rendering), a check in a layout does not run for every page transition, and Server Actions or Route Handlers under that layout are not protected by it at all.

lesson.heading: Sessions
lesson.body:
Two main strategies:
- **Stateless sessions**: the session data (user id, role, expiry) is signed or encrypted into a cookie, for example a JWT created with `jose`. No database lookup per request; revocation is hard until expiry.
- **Database sessions**: the cookie holds an opaque session id; the server looks it up. Easy revocation and device lists; costs a lookup (cache it per request with React `cache()`).

Cookie settings: `httpOnly` (no JS access, mitigates XSS token theft), `secure` (HTTPS only), `sameSite: 'lax'` (CSRF mitigation), a sensible `maxAge`, and `path: '/'`. In Next.js, cookies are set in Server Actions or Route Handlers with `(await cookies()).set(...)`, not in Server Components during render.

Libraries: Auth.js (NextAuth v5), Better Auth, Clerk, WorkOS, Supabase Auth and others handle OAuth, sessions and CSRF details; rolling your own is fine for learning but riskier in production.

lesson.heading: A Data Access Layer
lesson.body:
The pattern recommended in the Next.js auth guide is a **Data Access Layer (DAL)**: a server-only module that verifies the session and is the only place that queries protected data. Every page, action and handler calls it, so authorization cannot be forgotten.

The DAL returns **Data Transfer Objects** (DTOs) containing only the fields the caller may see, never raw database rows, which prevents leaking fields like password hashes or internal flags to Client Components through props.

lesson.heading: Authorization in the UI
lesson.body:
- Server Components can conditionally render admin-only UI after checking the session. That improves UX but is not security; the underlying data calls must also check.
- Client Components should receive only what the user may see. Hiding a button with a role flag in the client is cosmetic.
- Server Actions: verify the session and the user's permission for the specific resource (ownership, tenant, role) on every call.
- Route Handlers: same checks, plus proper status codes (401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden).
- Next.js also offers `forbidden()` and `unauthorized()` with `forbidden.tsx` and `unauthorized.tsx` files behind the experimental `authInterrupts` flag.

keyPoints: Next 16 renamed middleware.ts to proxy.ts with a proxy function; it runs on the Node.js runtime.
Use proxy for redirects, rewrites, headers and optimistic cookie checks; keep it fast.
CVE-2025-29927 showed why middleware or proxy must never be the only auth check.
Layout checks do not protect pages on client navigation, nor Server Actions and Route Handlers.
Session cookies should be httpOnly, secure and sameSite=lax; set them in actions or handlers.
Centralize authorization in a server-only Data Access Layer that returns DTOs.
Authorize per resource inside every Server Action and Route Handler.

questions.prompt: You upgrade to Next.js 16. What do you do with middleware.ts?
options: Rename it to proxy.ts and rename the exported function to proxy
questions.explanation: proxy.ts replaces middleware.ts. The logic stays the same; middleware.ts remains only for deprecated Edge runtime use.

questions.prompt: Which runtime does proxy.ts use in Next.js 16?
questions.explanation: proxy.ts runs on Node.js. Edge runtime interception still requires the deprecated middleware.ts.

questions.prompt: The dashboard layout checks the session and redirects if missing. Why is this insufficient?
options: Layouts do not re-render on client navigation, and actions and handlers below are not protected by it
redirect is not allowed in layouts
Layouts run only at build time
questions.explanation: Partial rendering skips shared layouts on navigation. Put checks in the data layer used by pages, actions and handlers.

questions.prompt: Which cookie attribute prevents JavaScript running on the page from reading the session token?
questions.explanation: httpOnly cookies are sent with requests but not exposed to document.cookie, limiting token theft through XSS.

questions.prompt: What should proxy.ts do for auth?
options: Validate the session against the database and load permissions
An optimistic check such as cookie presence, redirecting unauthenticated users early
questions.explanation: Proxy runs on every matched request including prefetches, so it should be fast and optimistic. Secure checks belong next to the data.

questions.prompt: Why does the DAL return a DTO instead of the database row?
options: To avoid leaking fields like password hashes or internal flags to callers and Client Components
Rows cannot be passed to components
questions.explanation: Returning only needed fields keeps sensitive data from accidentally crossing to the client.

questions.prompt: CVE-2025-29927 allowed attackers to bypass Next.js middleware with a crafted header, exposing apps that relied on it alone for authorization.
questions.explanation: The x-middleware-subrequest header could skip middleware on self-hosted apps. It was patched, and the lesson is defense in depth.

questions.prompt: You can set cookies inside a Server Component while it renders.
questions.explanation: Cookies can be read in Server Components but set only in Server Actions, Route Handlers or proxy, because HTTP headers may already be streaming.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: where must authorization be enforced for a protected 'delete project' feature?
options: In the Server Action that deletes the project
Only by hiding the delete button for non-owners
In any Route Handler exposing the same operation
In the data access function that performs the delete
questions.explanation: Every server entry point and the data layer must check. UI hiding and proxy are optimistic layers, not security.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: in proxy.ts, the exported ___ object with a matcher array limits which paths the proxy runs on.
questions.explanation: export const config = { matcher: [...] } scopes the proxy, typically excluding static assets.

questions.prompt: How would you implement authentication in a Next.js 16 App Router app?
questions.answer: I would use an established library (Auth.js, Better Auth or Clerk) unless there is a reason not to. Sign-in runs in a Server Action or Route Handler that verifies credentials or completes OAuth, then sets an httpOnly, secure, sameSite=lax session cookie, either an encrypted stateless token or an opaque id for a database session. proxy.ts does an optimistic check for the cookie on protected paths and redirects to login early. The real checks live in a server-only Data Access Layer: verifySession is wrapped in React cache to dedupe per request, and every data function checks ownership or role and returns DTOs. Server Actions and Route Handlers call the DAL too. Logout deletes the cookie (and the database session). I never rely on layout checks or hidden UI for security.

questions.prompt: Stateless JWT sessions vs database sessions: trade-offs?
questions.answer: Stateless sessions put signed or encrypted claims in the cookie. No lookup is needed per request, which is fast and scales easily, and works at the edge. But you cannot revoke a token before it expires without a denylist (which reintroduces state), claims like role can go stale, and cookie size limits what you can store. Database sessions store an opaque random id in the cookie and session data server-side: instant revocation, logout from all devices, session listing and fresh permissions, at the cost of a lookup per request, which can be cached per request or in Redis. Many apps use short-lived stateless tokens with refresh, or database sessions with a cache. For admin or financial apps I prefer database sessions for revocation.

questions.prompt: What would you use proxy.ts for, and what would you avoid doing in it?
questions.answer: I use it for request-level concerns that must happen before routing: redirects for moved URLs, locale detection and rewrites for i18n, A/B test bucketing via cookies and rewrites, adding security headers or a CSP nonce, bot or geo-based routing, and optimistic auth redirects based on cookie presence. I avoid heavy work since it runs on every matched request including prefetches: no database queries per request, no slow third-party calls, no full session validation or permission loading, and no business logic. I scope it with a matcher to skip static assets and images. Since Next 16 it runs on Node.js; the deprecated middleware.ts remains only for Edge needs.

chapters.title: Production: Deployment, Turbopack and Upgrading
chapters.summary: Deployment targets and self-hosting concerns, Turbopack as the default bundler, upgrading to Next.js 16, and production performance.

lesson.heading: Deployment options
lesson.body:
- **Managed platforms** (Vercel and others with Next.js support): ISR, caching, image optimization and streaming work without setup.
- **Node.js server**: `next build` then `next start`. Supports every feature.
- **Docker**: set `output: 'standalone'` so the build emits a minimal server with only the needed `node_modules`, which keeps images small.
- **Static export**: `output: 'export'` produces plain HTML, CSS and JS for any static host. You lose everything that needs a server: Server Actions, dynamic rendering, request-time APIs, proxy, ISR, and default image optimization.
- **Adapters**: Next 16 ships an alpha Build Adapters API so platforms can hook into the build output.

Environment variables: server-only vars are read at runtime, but `NEXT_PUBLIC_` vars are inlined at build time, so a Docker image built once cannot change them per environment without rebuilding (or reading them from the server and passing them down).

lesson.heading: Self-hosting at scale
lesson.body:
When you run several instances behind a load balancer:
- The default cache is in memory per instance, so ISR and `'use cache'` entries diverge between instances and invalidation only hits one. Configure a shared cache handler (`cacheHandler` / `cacheHandlers` in `next.config`, for example backed by Redis).
- Set a consistent `deploymentId` or build ID so instances agree, and handle version skew during rolling deploys.
- Server Action IDs are generated per build; clients on an old build calling a new server can fail, so mitigate skew and set a stable encryption key (`NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY`) across instances.
- Put a CDN in front for static assets, and make sure it respects the `Cache-Control` headers Next.js sends.
- Image optimization is CPU heavy; consider a dedicated loader or CDN.

lesson.heading: Turbopack
lesson.body:
Turbopack is a Rust-based incremental bundler. In Next.js 16 it is **stable and the default** for both `next dev` and `next build`, with 2-5x faster production builds and up to 10x faster Fast Refresh reported by the Next.js team. It caches work at the function level, so only affected modules are recomputed. File system caching for dev (persisting compiler artifacts across restarts) is in beta behind `experimental.turbopackFileSystemCacheForDev`.

To keep webpack, run `next dev --webpack` and `next build --webpack`. A project with a custom `webpack()` function in `next.config` will not have it applied by Turbopack, so migrate the needed parts (loaders via `turbopack.rules`, aliases via `turbopack.resolveAlias`) or opt out. Turbopack configuration lives at the top-level `turbopack` key (it moved out of `experimental`). Babel configs are detected and applied automatically.

lesson.heading: Upgrading to Next.js 16
lesson.body:
Run `npx @next/codemod@canary upgrade latest`, then check the breaking changes:
- Node.js 20.9+ and TypeScript 5.1+ are required.
- Synchronous access to `params`, `searchParams`, `cookies()`, `headers()` and `draftMode()` is removed: await them.
- `middleware.ts` becomes `proxy.ts`.
- Every parallel route slot needs a `default.js`.
- `revalidateTag` needs a second profile argument.
- `next lint` is removed (use ESLint or Biome directly), and `next build` no longer lints.
- AMP, `serverRuntimeConfig` and `publicRuntimeConfig` are removed; use env variables.
- `experimental.ppr` and `experimental.dynamicIO` are replaced by `cacheComponents`.
- `next/image` defaults changed (`qualities: [75]`, 4-hour `minimumCacheTTL`), `images.domains` and `priority` are deprecated.
- React Compiler support is stable via `reactCompiler: true` (not on by default; it slows builds because it uses Babel).

lesson.heading: Production performance checklist
lesson.body:
- Keep `'use client'` at the leaves and move heavy libraries to Server Components.
- Load heavy client-only widgets lazily with `next/dynamic`.
- Analyze bundles and remove large dependencies; use `optimizePackageImports` for icon libraries if needed.
- Make the static shell large with Cache Components; stream dynamic parts with Suspense.
- Use next/image with correct `sizes` and eager loading for the LCP image; use next/font.
- Avoid request waterfalls; colocate the server with the database.
- Monitor with `instrumentation.ts` (OpenTelemetry, `onRequestError` for error reporting) and real-user Web Vitals via `useReportWebVitals`.

output: 'export' drops all server features: actions, dynamic rendering, proxy, ISR and default image optimization.
NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables are baked in at build time.
Multi-instance self-hosting needs a shared cache handler, consistent build IDs and a stable Server Actions encryption key.
Turbopack is the default bundler for dev and build in Next 16; opt out with --webpack.

Monitor with instrumentation.ts and Web Vitals; keep client bundles small.

questions.explanation: Static export produces files at build time, so prerendered pages work but anything needing a running server does not.

questions.prompt: What does output: 'standalone' do?
options: Emits a minimal Node.js server with only the required dependencies, ideal for Docker
Bundles the app as a single HTML file
questions.explanation: Standalone output traces the files and node_modules actually used, producing a small deployable folder.

options: Only that instance's in-memory cache is invalidated; the others keep serving old data
questions.explanation: The default cache is per process. A shared cache handler such as Redis keeps instances consistent.

questions.prompt: How do you build a Next.js 16 app with webpack instead of Turbopack?
questions.explanation: Turbopack is the default; the --webpack flag on dev and build opts out.

questions.prompt: A Docker image is built once and deployed to staging and production. NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL differs per environment. What happens?
options: Each environment reads its own value at runtime
The client bundle contains the value present at build time in both environments
Next.js fetches it from the server on load
questions.explanation: NEXT_PUBLIC_ values are inlined during next build. Use server-read runtime variables passed down, or build per environment.

questions.prompt: Which Next.js 16 change requires code edits in most older App Router apps?
options: Removal of synchronous params, searchParams, cookies() and headers() access
questions.explanation: The temporary synchronous compatibility from Next 15 was removed; these must be awaited.

questions.prompt: In Next.js 16, next build still runs ESLint automatically.
questions.explanation: next lint was removed and next build no longer lints. Run ESLint or Biome directly, for example in CI.

questions.prompt: React Compiler is enabled by default in new Next.js 16 projects.
questions.explanation: reactCompiler is stable but opt-in, because it relies on Babel and increases compile times.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: breaking changes or requirements in Next.js 16.
options: Every parallel route slot needs default.js
questions.explanation: Server Components remain the foundation. The others are listed in the Next.js 16 release notes.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the file at the project root used to register OpenTelemetry and onRequestError hooks is ___.ts.
questions.explanation: instrumentation.ts exports register() and onRequestError for observability.

questions.prompt: What do you need to consider when self-hosting Next.js instead of using Vercel?
questions.answer: Use next start or output: 'standalone' in Docker behind a reverse proxy that supports streaming (disable response buffering, for example in Nginx). With more than one instance, configure a shared cache handler for ISR and 'use cache' entries, a consistent deploymentId, and a stable NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY, and plan for version skew during rolling deploys. Put a CDN in front for static assets and respect Cache-Control. Image optimization is CPU intensive; use a dedicated image CDN or loader if traffic is high. NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables are inlined at build time. Add observability with instrumentation.ts, health checks, and graceful shutdown. Keep Next.js patched, which matters for advisories like the 2025 middleware bypass.

questions.prompt: What is Turbopack and how does it differ from webpack in Next.js 16?
questions.answer: Turbopack is an incremental bundler written in Rust, built into Next.js. It is the default for next dev and next build in Next 16. Its engine memoizes work at the level of individual functions and modules, so after a change it recomputes only what is affected, which gives faster Fast Refresh and builds; file system caching for dev persists that work across restarts (beta). Configuration is under the top-level turbopack key: rules for loaders (it supports many webpack loaders) and resolveAlias. It does not run a custom webpack() config function, so projects with heavy webpack customization either migrate those pieces or opt out with --webpack. Babel configs are detected and applied automatically.

questions.prompt: How would you plan an upgrade of a large app from Next.js 14 to 16?
questions.answer: Upgrade in steps: 14 to 15, then 16, with tests and visual checks at each step. Run the official codemods (upgrade latest, async request APIs, middleware-to-proxy, next-lint-to-eslint-cli). Review every place that relied on implicit caching, since fetch and GET handlers became uncached in 15: decide explicitly what to cache, ideally with Cache Components and 'use cache' plus cacheLife and cacheTag. Update React to 19 and check third-party libraries for compatibility. Fix breaking changes: awaited params and cookies, proxy.ts, default.js for parallel slots, two-argument revalidateTag, removed runtime config, image default changes. Check whether custom webpack config blocks Turbopack builds. Roll out behind a canary deployment and watch error rates and Web Vitals.
